beats.text: For 30 years, Democrats kept saying Texas was about to turn blue.
It kept not happening.
In 2018, Beto O'Rourke came within about three points of Ted Cruz.
In 2020, Donald Trump won Texas by under six.
Then in 2024, Trump won it by almost *14*.
He even won Starr County on the Mexican border, which is 97% Hispanic and had not
voted Republican for president since 1892.
Hispanic voters, the group Democrats had counted on, were shifting right.
Then came *2026*.
In the Republican primary, Attorney General Ken Paxton beat the
four-term senator John Cornyn, with President Trump's endorsement.
On November the 3rd, the Democrat James Talarico, a former teacher, beat Paxton
by more than 10 points, and the Democrat Gina Hinojosa beat Governor Greg Abbott
by about seven. She will be the first Latina governor in Texas history.
So *why*?
You have heard the national explanation.
A midterm year and an unpopular president.
That's real.
People on both sides say so.
But it does not explain why Texas swung *harder* than almost anywhere else.
So listen to Texas Republicans themselves.
The morning after, the head of the Texas Young Republicans
called Paxton "a terrible candidate."
A Republican who lost his own statewide race said people were "tired of the Republicans being in office."
A Texas political scientist blamed what he called the party's "lazy arrogance."
Democrats point to other things: everyday costs, public schools,
and the fight over school vouchers.
And the people who actually decided it? A lot of them were
Republicans, splitting their tickets.
One Republican pollster put it this way: Paxton gave them *permission*.
Remember the one-party trap I promised you?
Here's the whole thing.
Stage one: the party gets so dominant that the primary is the only race
that matters, so the real fight moves inside the party, and it *splits*.
Stage two: the winner of that fight is someone a lot of the party's
own voters can't stand.
Stage three: the *Switchers* walk.
Not to the other party's ideas. Away from their own party's choice.
1961: Democrats split.
Liberal Democrats refused to back their own conservative candidate,
and John Tower slipped through.
1978: the Democratic nominee had just knocked out his party's sitting
governor in the primary, and Bill Clements won by less than one point.
2026: Republicans tore into each other in the most expensive
Senate primary on record.
Paxton won it, and Republican Switchers walked.
Both parties, same *trap*.
And here's the part nobody tells you.
After Tower's crack in 1961, it took *33* more years for
Republicans to win everything.
So was Tuesday a flip, or just a crack in the banner?
That depends on what Texas Republicans do next, because the trap has an exit.
You just have to remember you can *lose*.
Six flags, two one-party eras.
Both ended the same way.
So this was never really a story about Democrats or Republicans.
It's a story about Texans who refuse to be taken for *granted*.
In Texas, the moment a party thinks it can't lose, it starts to.
And hey, give it 30 years.
Somebody will make a video asking why Texas was always *Democrat*.
